title: Hands in prayer
hookLine: folded on the chest, below the navel, or at the sides, depending on school

cards: Stand at the back of a big mosque during prayer and watch the hands. One man has his right hand over his left, low, just under the navel. The man beside him holds his higher, near the chest.
Two places down, someone's arms hang straight at his sides. Nobody turns to correct anybody. They bow together, go down together, rise together.
Same prayer, same imam, three different pairs of hands. Each of them learned it from somewhere. Today, why.

teach.b: Start with a report the schools share. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahl ibn Sa'd says people were told to place the right hand on the left forearm in prayer. Holding, called qabd, has a text behind it.
But the text leaves a question: where? It says right over left.

teach.h: THE TEXT DOESN'T SAY HOW HIGH.
teach.b: It doesn't say how high. So the schools weighed other reports, and different answers came out. Hanafi scholars teach men to hold the hands below the navel.
Shafi'i scholars place them below the chest and above the navel. In the Hanbali school, below the navel is a well-known view, with room for other places.
And some readers point to reports placing the hands on the chest itself.

teach.h: SADL: THE ARMS AT THE SIDES.
teach.b: Then the arms at the sides, called sadl, letting the hands hang. In the Maliki school, a report from Imam Malik is read as disliking holding in the obligatory prayers, and in Maliki mosques you may see arms down.

teach.h: HANDS ARE A MAP OF TEACHERS.
teach.b: The Ja'fari school teaches the arms at the sides, hands resting on the thighs, and so do the Zaydis and the Ibadis.
Each of these is a reading of reports from the same Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, passed down by different teachers.
In the same row, the man with low hands and the man with hanging arms are each praying as their own school teaches. A stranger's hands aren't a mistake. They're a map of who taught him.

how: In the standing of prayer, Hanafis hold the right hand over the left below the navel, Shafi'is below the chest, Hanbalis below the navel or as their school allows; Malikis following Malik's reported view, and Ja'fari, Zaydi and Ibadi Muslims, pray with their arms at their sides.

o: a gesture of blessing an imam makes over the row
where the hands rest in prayer, which differs from school to school
holding prayer beads in the right hand all through the prayer

games.q: hands in prayer — tap the pairs.
p: below the chest, above the navel

s: praying with the arms at the sides is a modern innovation
it is the teaching of the Ja'fari, Zaydi and Ibadi schools, and of Malikis reading a report from Imam Malik.
Sahl ibn Sa'd's report says the right hand goes over the left
it does, in Sahih al-Bukhari, and it doesn't say how high.
every Sunni school puts the hands in the same place
Hanafi below the navel, Shafi'i below the chest, and the Hanbali school allows more than one place.

games.q: you're praying in a crowded row. the man beside you lets his arms hang at his sides. what do you do?
o: keep praying; his hands follow his school.
games.why: letting the arms hang is the teaching of Malikis and of the Ja'fari, Zaydi and Ibadi schools. he is praying as his school teaches.

practice: If you pray, stand for a moment, place your hands where you learned to, and ask who taught you: a parent, an imam, a video, a friend.

If you don't, let your hands rest wherever they fall, feel their weight, and think of someone who taught you to do something with them, tie a knot, hold a pen, knead dough. Stay with that person for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Hands in prayer. Held below the navel, below the chest, on the chest, or at the sides, depending on school; each passed down by a teacher. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: letting hang; in prayer, standing with the arms at the sides. its partner word is qabd, holding.

carryVoice: Your line: different hands. One row, many teachers. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 740 (Sahl ibn Sa'd: right hand on the left forearm)
